items.title: Move the Fourier window with the Bragg spot, and strain maps stop failing
items.dek: Ying Han and Yuan Tian report that measuring strain from atomic-resolution electron-microscope images — how far a crystal's lattice has been stretched — fails 27% of the time, and that letting the analysis window follow the diffraction spot cuts that to 11.5%.
items.why_it_matters: A strain map that fails silently is worse than no measurement at all: geometric phase analysis returns a smooth, plausible displacement field when its fixed filter has lost the diffraction spot, so a dropped reflection reads as strain that is not there, and nothing in the output says which it was. Tracking the spot also produces a per-pixel confidence number, which is the first thing that lets a reader of the map tell a real lattice gradient from an artefact of the filter.
items.background_md: A crystal lattice under strain has its atomic planes pushed closer together or further apart, and that shift changes the electronic band structure — which is why strained silicon is a deliberate process step rather than an accident. Measuring it means resolving a spacing change of a few picometres across a field of view hundreds of nanometres wide. The usual route is reciprocal space: take a Fourier transform of an atomic-resolution image, select one Bragg reflection with a band-pass filter, and read the lattice displacement out of how that reflection's phase varies across the image.
items.deeper_md:
Geometric phase analysis (GPA) puts a fixed aperture around one Bragg reflection in the Fourier transform and treats the phase of the filtered signal as a displacement field. The aperture radius is a direct trade: wide enough that the reflection stays inside it as the lattice rotates or strains, narrow enough to reject noise. Past a few per cent of strain, or across a misoriented grain, the reflection leaves the aperture and GPA computes a displacement field out of whatever noise was left inside it.

Geometric phase tracking moves the aperture to follow the reflection at every pixel, so a narrow aperture can be used everywhere. Across 13,795 simulated and experimental images the authors put GPA's failure rate at 27% and theirs at 11.5%, with accuracy "up to" 335× better — an upper bound whose imaging condition the abstract does not name, and the simulated and experimental failure rates are not reported separately.

The underlying fragility is not in dispute. Peters and co-workers showed in 2015 that in a compound crystal, where the unit cell holds more than one atom, GPA reports strain at a structural interface where there is none, from an extra phase term that has nothing to do with the lattice spacing at all.

glossary.definition: A bright spot in the Fourier transform of a lattice image, one per family of parallel atomic planes; its position gives the plane spacing and the phase of its signal gives where the planes sit.
Strain mapping by band-pass filtering one Bragg reflection out of an image and reading lattice displacement from how the filtered signal's phase drifts across the field of view.
The filter window placed around a chosen Bragg reflection; its radius sets both how much noise is rejected and how far the reflection may move before the measurement stops meaning anything.
In a thick specimen, electron waves interfere strongly enough that a Bragg reflection can vanish entirely at certain thicknesses, removing the signal a phase-based method depends on.

items.fab_angle: The same trap sits inside any pitch or linewidth pulled out of an image by band-pass filtering: fix the filter around the pitch you expected, and a real pitch drift moves the signal out of the window, so the number that comes back is your assumption rather than the print.

sources.title: From phase analysis to phase tracking: a robust approach to atomic-scale strain mapping

items.title: One etch pattern makes the membrane a mirror and a phonon shield
items.dek: Alexander Jung, Anastasiia Ciers and co-authors patterned a thin silicon-nitride membrane with high-index nanopillars that reflect 99.82% of a tightly focused 1550 nm laser beam while also trapping one mechanical vibration mode at a quality-factor-times-frequency product of 2×10¹⁴ hertz.
items.why_it_matters: Cavity optomechanics has had to choose between two incompatible thicknesses: a reflector thick enough to return a tightly focused beam is mechanically lossy, and a membrane thin enough to ring for a long time barely reflects. Folding the optical and the mechanical structure into one lithographic pattern removes the choice, and it removes the usual workaround as well — the beam waist no longer has to be enlarged to match a bigger mirror, which is what has been setting how short the cavity can be.
items.background_md: A membrane a hundred nanometres thick, held under tension, is one of the quietest mechanical oscillators available: tension stores most of the vibrational energy, so the material's own internal friction acts on a smaller share of it and the mode decays slowly. Two things spoil that. Clamping at the edge forces curvature there and leaks energy into the substrate, which is why these membranes are patterned with a phononic crystal — a periodic density modulation whose band gap confines the mode away from the edge. And a film that thin barely reflects, so it makes a poor mirror for the cavity meant to read it out.
items.deeper_md:
The pillars do two jobs because the period that opens a phononic band gap also forms a photonic crystal. Reflection comes from flat-band guided resonances in the pillar array rather than from film thickness, so a 50 µm-diameter array returns 99.82(1)% for a 7 µm beam waist; combining two guided resonances widens the high-reflectivity band to roughly 100 nm around 1550 nm, which matters because a single guided resonance is narrow enough that a fabrication error detunes it.

The mechanical figure needs reading carefully. A Q·f of 2×10¹⁴ Hz is in the same class as the soft-clamped silicon-nitride membranes Tsaturyan and co-workers reported in 2017, which already exceeded 10¹⁴ Hz with no optical function at all. The nearest combined predecessor — an 88.5 nm membrane carrying separate photonic and phononic patterns — reached a higher 99.89% reflectivity but only Q = 2.9×10⁷. What is new is holding both at once for a beam waist of a few micrometres, and the claim rests on fabricated arrays rather than a yield distribution.

glossary.definition: Mechanical quality factor multiplied by resonance frequency; it counts how many cycles a mode rings before thermal noise overwhelms it, which is why it is quoted instead of Q alone.
Stretching a membrane stores most of its vibrational energy as tension rather than as bending of the material, so the material's internal friction acts on a smaller fraction of the energy.

A mode that propagates inside a patterned slab and couples to free-space light; on resonance the slab's transmission interferes destructively, which is how a sub-wavelength film reflects nearly everything.
A range of mechanical frequencies a periodic structure will not transmit, used here to trap one vibration away from the clamped edge where energy drains into the substrate.

items.fab_angle: Both functions now ride on a single mask layer, which removes an overlay step and couples two tolerances: a critical-dimension error moves the optical resonance and the mechanical band gap together, so one etch bias has to satisfy a photonic period and a phononic one at the same time.

items.title: Grow the perovskite sheet wide enough and you can skip the resist
items.dek: Shankeerthan Kalyanasundaram and co-authors grew single-layer hybrid perovskite crystals over 1,000 square micrometres — wide enough to contact through a shadow mask instead of photolithography, whose solvents attack the material — and measured 0.2 picowatts of standby power at 5 volts.
items.why_it_matters: Flake size is the reason this material class has stayed on the bench: at a few micrometres across, the only way to land an electrode is lithography, and lithography means spin-coating a resist and developing it in solvents that take the crystal apart. A flake wide enough for a stencil converts a materials-compatibility problem into a geometry one, and that is why the dark current measured here is 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹³ amps instead of whatever a developer-damaged surface would have leaked.
items.background_md: A two-dimensional hybrid perovskite is an inorganic metal-halide sheet one octahedron thick, separated from the next sheet by a layer of large organic cations. The organic spacer is what makes the material easy to deposit from solution and also what makes it fragile: the structure is held together by ionic and hydrogen bonds rather than a covalent lattice, so polar solvents take it apart and ambient humidity degrades unprotected flakes within hours. Every process step after deposition therefore has to avoid water, alcohols and the developer chemistry that a resist requires.
items.deeper_md:
Solution growth normally stacks these sheets instead of spreading them, because out-of-plane growth wins: nucleation is poorly controlled and finished layers aggregate, capping lateral size at a few micrometres. The authors add alcohol co-solvents plus an amine to a ternary solvent system; by their molecular-dynamics and quantum-chemical calculations the longer-chain alcohols change how the precursor is solvated, and solvent volatility keeps edge-driven precursor transport running longer during the anneal. Monolayers exceed 1,000 µm², and the recipe transfers across spacer cations, across Cu²⁺, Mn²⁺ and Pb²⁺, and across Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻.

The device numbers follow from the size rather than from new physics. Shadow-masked contacts on isolated ultrathin (PEA)₂PbI₄ channels leak 10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹³ A, about 0.2 pW at 5 V and 250× less standby power than a drop-cast film, at a light-to-dark current ratio of 4.3×10² — modest for a detector. Two caveats: this is a preprint with no reported stability data, and Seitz and co-workers found unencapsulated (PEA)₂PbI₄ degrades within hours in air unless it is capped with hexagonal boron nitride.

glossary.definition: A layered hybrid crystal: one sheet of metal-halide octahedra built from M and X, sandwiched between two layers of bulky organic cations A, which is why the sheets separate so readily.
Evaporating metal through a pre-cut self-supporting aperture held against the sample, so electrodes are defined without ever putting resist, developer or solvent on the surface.
The current a photodetector passes with no light on it; it fixes the standby power and the smallest optical signal the device can distinguish from its own leakage.
Photocurrent under illumination divided by dark current — the detector's usable contrast, here 4.3×10², which is low beside a silicon photodiode.

items.fab_angle: This is the case where coat–expose–develop is itself the defect mechanism, so the pattern has to be defined before the film exists or through a stencil afterwards. Shadow masking costs resolution, because the aperture must be self-supporting, and that trade is the whole reason flake width mattered.

items.title: An accelerator datapath that speeds up as the weights get smaller
items.dek: Faraz Tahmasebi and co-authors built a matrix-multiply datapath for language models whose throughput rises as weight precision falls, by recoding each low-bit integer weight into radix-4 digits so that one digit — not one bit — produces a partial product.
items.why_it_matters: On a GPU, quantising weights to two or three bits saves memory and nothing else: the weights are expanded back to 16-bit floating point before the multiply, so the arithmetic takes exactly as long as it did. A datapath whose partial-product count scales with digits rather than with operand width is what converts a compression ratio into a throughput ratio, and it changes what a quantiser should be optimising — a per-channel bit-width assignment now buys silicon time, not only DRAM traffic.
items.background_md: Weight-only quantisation stores a transformer's weights as low-bit integers and leaves its activations in floating point, so the dominant kernel becomes a floating-point-by-integer matrix multiply. The attraction is memory: during single-token decoding almost all the time goes into reading weights out of DRAM, so a weight four times smaller costs four times less traffic. The arithmetic is where it stops paying. A multiplier array is built for a fixed operand width, so feeding it a 3-bit weight occupies a fraction of the hardware and takes exactly as long as feeding it a 16-bit one.
items.deeper_md:
Radix-4 recoding splits a P-bit weight into ⌈P/2⌉ digits, each selecting one of {0, m, 2m, 3m} through a 4:1 multiplexer, so the partial-product count roughly halves and one integer adder tree performs both the multiply and the accumulate, with no per-cell multiplier. Only 3m needs an addition, computed once per row at the array edge. INT3 would waste half of a two-bit lane, so the high bits of a weight pair share a lane: three lanes for two weights, 10.67 instead of 8 MAC/cycle at K=16, for about 1.3% more area.

Synthesised in NanGate 15 nm at 3.43 mm² including 1.2 MB of SRAM, it reports 1.56× the whole-chip throughput per area of AxCore and 1.42× that of FIGLUT on 3-bit linear GEMMs. The caveats are the authors' own: synthesis rather than silicon, re-implemented baselines, attention and memory modelled rather than measured, and decode batches under 16 leaving the 16-row array memory-bound. LLaMA-2-7B WikiText-2 perplexity is 5.85 at 3 bits and 8.77 at 2 bits against 5.47 in FP16 — better than GPTQ's 6.14 and 32.61, but still 1.6× the FP16 figure at 2 bits with no fine-tuning.

glossary.definition: A matrix multiply with floating-point activations and integer weights; it is the kernel weight-only quantisation produces, and no mainstream GPU executes it without first expanding the weights.
Reading a binary multiplier two bits at a time so each digit contributes one partial product instead of two, halving the rows an adder tree has to sum.
One shifted copy of the multiplicand selected by a digit of the multiplier; a multiplier's area and delay are set by how many of these must be added together.
The exponential of a language model's average per-token loss on held-out text; lower is better, and a few tenths is the usual currency for judging a quantisation scheme.

items.title: Ray-tracing hardware idles because its buffers are sized per warp
items.dek: Junrui Pan and co-authors report, in a paper on the MICRO 2026 programme, that GPU ray-tracing units sit underused because on-chip buffers are allocated to whole groups of threads, and that splitting those buffers down to individual rays raises performance 1.91× for 0.19% more area.
items.why_it_matters: Ray tracing is the workload that breaks the GPU's central bargain: lanes execute in lockstep, and rays do not, because each one visits a different number of tree nodes and terminates at a different depth. When a buffer is reserved for a whole warp, the slowest ray in it holds storage the finished rays cannot release, so the number of warps in flight is capped by buffer capacity rather than by available traversal throughput. Allocating per ray decouples the two.
items.background_md: A GPU executes threads in fixed groups — a warp — that share one instruction pointer, which is what makes the hardware cheap: a single fetch and decode serve dozens of lanes. The arrangement pays off when the lanes do the same thing and collapses when they do not, because a branch only some lanes take must be run with the rest masked off and wasted. Ray tracing is the hardest case. Each ray walks its own path down an acceleration structure, a tree over scene geometry that lets a ray skip the triangles it cannot possibly hit.
items.deeper_md:
The claim is about resource management rather than arithmetic. Buffers inside the traversal unit are partitioned at warp granularity, so a warp holds its allocation until its last ray finishes and the unit runs out of buffer entries long before it runs out of traversal throughput. Partitioning down to a single ray, plus the bookkeeping needed to track per-ray ownership, lets more warps stay resident without adding capacity — which lifts both unit utilisation and the number of outstanding memory requests, since divergent rays are also what generates memory-level parallelism in the first place.

Read the 1.91× average and 0.19% area as simulation. Nobody outside a vendor has the real buffer sizes: the same group's open-source RayFlex RTL exists precisely because the datapath is otherwise unpublished, and the comparable prefetching result in this space, TTP, reached 1.48× on the Vulkan-sim 2.0 cycle-level model by reusing the traversal stack to fetch tree nodes early. TTP attacks the same memory-bound traversal by hiding latency; this attacks it by not reserving capacity it cannot use. The paper is listed for the 59th MICRO, 31 October to 4 November in Athens.

glossary.definition: The group of threads a GPU issues together under one instruction pointer; divergence inside a warp costs execution slots, because lanes that did not take a branch are masked off rather than reused.
Single-instruction, multiple-thread: the execution model where one instruction stream drives many lanes, trading per-lane flexibility for a fetch and decode shared across all of them.
A tree of nested bounding boxes built over scene geometry, which a ray descends so that it only tests triangles inside boxes it actually intersects.
How many independent memory requests a unit keeps outstanding at once; it is what hides DRAM latency, so a design that caps concurrency caps achievable bandwidth too.

items.title: Classic McEliece's margin now turns on a cost model, not a theorem
items.dek: Ramses Fernandez assesses this year's structural attacks on Classic McEliece — the code-based public-key scheme built on binary Goppa codes — and finds the same key-recovery computation costs anywhere across about thirty bits depending on which cost model it is charged against.
items.why_it_matters: A security level is a claim about work, and work is only defined once you have agreed what an operation costs. For four of the five parameter sets the key-recovery estimate sits at least 82 bits under the target of its NIST category under every model considered, so the accounting does not change the verdict. For the smallest, mceliece348864, the shortfall is 26 to 51 bits — the same size as the spread between models, which makes its status a function of the convention chosen.
items.background_md: Code-based cryptography hides a structured error-correcting code inside a scrambled generator matrix. Whoever knows the structure can decode; everyone else faces decoding a random-looking linear code, which is NP-hard in general. Classic McEliece builds on binary Goppa codes, and its security argument has two legs: that generic decoding is hard, and that the published matrix looks random enough that the Goppa structure cannot be read back out of it. A structural attack goes after the second leg, and the second leg has far less theory standing behind it than the first.
items.deeper_md:
Three structural results are in play. Randriambololona's syzygy distinguisher (EUROCRYPT 2025) is slightly subexponential in the error-correcting capacity t, and Germany's BSI puts its cost on the recommended parameter sets at 2^683 or more. Hemmert and Wiemers' higher-order-vanishing distinguisher at CRYPTO 2026 comes in at 2^550 or more. The Holdout/Hermite distinguisher of Ghoshal, Ishai, Jain and Sun runs in n^O(log n) and costs 2^114 to 2^124 bit operations across the five sets, which is the one that matters.

Turning a distinguisher into a key recovery needs a large sparse linear-algebra step, and that is where the thirty bits live: Weis's operation count puts one run at 2^89.4 for mceliece348864, while charging for memory pushes the larger sets to 2^128.1, and some routes need up to roughly 1,400 runs.

None of it is a break, and Fernandez says so. The four load-bearing assumptions were tested only at about 10⁷ unknowns where a full-size run has 2^38 to 2^42, and the solved challenges are small instances — Saarinen's TII-254 took 27.2 GPU-hours on NVIDIA GH200s and its own paper says it does not threaten a real parameter set.

glossary.definition: An algebraic error-correcting code defined by a polynomial and a list of field elements; knowing both lets you decode efficiently, and the public key is a scrambled parity-check matrix meant to hide them.
An algorithm that only tells a real public key apart from a random matrix faster than chance; it decrypts nothing by itself, but it shows the key is not random and usually precedes recovery.
Attack cost quoted as a count of elementary operations; because a memory access and an arithmetic operation are not the same price, two defensible accounting rules can differ by tens of bits.
Solving a very large system whose matrix is almost all zeros; its cost is dominated by moving rows through memory rather than by arithmetic, which is exactly why the memory charge is contested.

items.title: Cross-entropy stops producing a gradient at a logit margin of 16.6
items.dek: Jonathan Barron, Dan Gnanapragasam and Michael Tschannen show that the standard cross-entropy loss stops producing a gradient on the correct class once that class's score leads the rest by about 16.6 in float32, because adding e^(−16.6) to 1.0 rounds straight back to 1.0.
items.why_it_matters: The failure is silent and asymmetric: the non-target gradients keep flowing until the exponential itself underflows near a margin of 88, so the gradients stop summing to zero and the loss quietly begins pushing logits apart rather than balancing them. Shifting only the largest logit to zero and computing the margin as a log-sum-exp over the remainder restores a nonzero target gradient at the same operation count, in the one function every training framework already calls on every step.
items.background_md: Softmax turns a vector of scores into probabilities by exponentiating and normalising, and cross-entropy then measures the negative log probability of the correct class. Both are evaluated in finite precision, and the standard stability trick is to subtract the largest score before exponentiating, which bounds the exponentials but does nothing about rounding. Floating point carries a fixed number of significant bits, so adding a very small number to 1.0 returns exactly 1.0 once that number falls below the unit round-off — about 2⁻²⁴ in float32, 2⁻⁸ in bfloat16.
items.deeper_md:
Write the target-class loss as softplus(−m), where m is the margin between the target logit and the log-sum-exp of the others. The gradient on the target is −e^(−m)/(1+e^(−m)); the denominator is computed as 1 + e^(−m), and once e^(−m) falls under the unit round-off the sum is exactly 1.0 and the target's contribution is lost. The cliff lands at m ≈ 5.5 in bfloat16, 16.6 in float32 and 36.7 in float64, while the non-target gradients survive to m ≈ 88 in float32.

It shows up in training. On a modular-addition task without weight decay, a spike at the float32 cliff drops standard cross-entropy's test accuracy from 61% to 23% where the fixed version reaches 85%; with AdamW the margin instead plateaus near log(1/ε), about 18.4 at ε = 1e-8. A second bug, in soft-target distillation, leaves a residual gradient near 1e-3 in bfloat16 when student and teacher logits are identical, because the two softmaxes are taken separately and then subtracted.

The authors' own limitation is the one to keep: margins this large and teacher gaps this small are uncommon in large-scale training, so this is a high-confidence-prediction and distillation fix, not a general speedup.

glossary.definition: The gap between the correct class's score and the combined score of all the others, taken as a log-sum-exp; it is the single quantity the loss and its gradient actually depend on.
The largest relative error one floating-point operation can introduce — about 2⁻²⁴ in float32 — which is why adding anything smaller than that to 1.0 changes nothing at all.
log Σ e^xᵢ and log(1+e^x): the two reformulations that let a softmax loss be evaluated without forming a huge exponential, and the exact place the rounding happens.

The pattern where a network memorises its training set and only generalises much later, spending a long stretch of training at very large logit margins — precisely the regime this rounding bug lives in.

foundations.subtitle: Two polymers that will not mix, tied together so they cannot get further apart than one chain is long — and the coarse guide pattern that tells them which way to point.
foundations.tldr: A block copolymer is two incompatible polymers joined end to end. Heat it and the two halves try to separate, but the covalent joint means they cannot get further apart than a chain is long, so they settle into stripes or dots whose spacing is set by molecular weight rather than by a lens. Directed self-assembly uses a coarse lithographic pattern to tell those stripes which way to run, and then spends most of its effort fighting the defects that thermodynamics leaves behind.

sections.heading: A pitch that comes from chemistry instead of optics
sections.body_md:
Everything about lithographic resolution is expensive. Half-pitch scales as wavelength over numerical aperture, and buying either costs a scanner. A block copolymer sidesteps the whole equation, because the size of the features it forms has nothing to do with light.

Take polystyrene and poly(methyl methacrylate), chain them together into one molecule, and spin the result onto a wafer. The two blocks are mutually insoluble. Given enough thermal energy to move, they separate — but each polystyrene segment is tied to a PMMA segment, so the separation cannot run further than the molecules are long. What you get is a periodic pattern whose period is set by the degree of polymerisation: lamellar stripes, or hexagonally packed cylinders, at tens of nanometres, from a hotplate.

The catch is in the next three sections. The pattern has a pitch but no orientation, no registration to anything already on the wafer, and a defect density several orders of magnitude above what a fab will accept.
sections.deeper_md: Two numbers govern the first part. Microphase separation requires χN above roughly 10.5, where χ is the Flory–Huggins interaction parameter per monomer contact and N is the degree of polymerisation. The natural full period scales as L₀ ≈ χ^(1/6)·N^(2/3), and the usable feature is about half of L₀. Those two together are a squeeze: shrinking the feature means shrinking N, and shrinking N means raising χ to stay above the ordering threshold. For PS-b-PMMA, χ ≈ 0.039 at 150 °C, which puts the floor near a 22 nm pitch — an 11 nm half-pitch — and is the reason the field spent a decade looking for more incompatible pairs.

sections.heading: Why they separate into stripes and not into two puddles
sections.body_md:
Mix polystyrene and PMMA as separate polymers and they do what oil and water do: they demix completely, into two bulk phases with one interface between them. That is macrophase separation, and it is useless for patterning.

The covalent bond joining the two blocks is what converts it into something useful. The blocks still want to minimise contact with each other, which drives them apart; the joint forbids them from ever being more than a molecule apart, which caps the domain size. The equilibrium is a compromise between interfacial energy, which wants fewer and flatter interfaces, and chain stretching, which resists being pulled out straight. The result is periodic — microphase separation.

The composition sets the shape. Roughly equal volume fractions give lamellae, which project as line-space. Skew the ratio and the minority block retracts into cylinders, then into spheres, which project as holes. That is why the same chemistry can be sold as a pitch-splitter for lines and as a hole-shrink for contacts.
sections.deeper_md: χ does more than set the ordering threshold; it sets the interfacial width between domains, which scales roughly as the inverse square root of χ. A sharper interface means less line-edge roughness in the transferred pattern, so high-χ materials are attractive for two independent reasons — smaller features and cleaner edges. This is also why the order–disorder transition temperature matters operationally: χ falls as temperature rises, so an anneal hot enough to give the chains mobility can be hot enough to disorder a marginal material. Jacobs and co-workers exploited exactly that, annealing near the transition to get registration that a lower-temperature bake could not.

sections.heading: Direction has to come from outside the film
sections.body_md:
Left alone, a block copolymer film forms fingerprint patterns: correct pitch, random orientation, grains a few periods wide. A circuit needs lines that run one way and sit in known places, so the direction is supplied by a lithographic pre-pattern — which is the "directed" in directed self-assembly, and the reason this is a lithography technique rather than a chemistry demonstration.

There are two ways to do it. Graphoepitaxy etches physical trenches two to five times the final critical dimension, makes the trench floor chemically neutral to both blocks, and treats one sidewall so it preferentially wets one of them. The copolymer fills the trench and registers off that wall, subdividing it into several lines. Chemoepitaxy keeps the surface flat and patterns chemistry instead: a stripe of cross-linked polystyrene beside a neutral brush. The polystyrene block anchors to the stripe and the rest of the pattern counts outward from it.

Either way, one coarse printed feature yields several finer ones. That is density multiplication, and it is the point.
sections.deeper_md: The two routes fail differently, and that is how to choose between them. Graphoepitaxy reuses processes a fab already has, and typically needs fewer steps, but the trench width has to be commensurate with L₀ — an integer number of periods, or the film is frustrated — and any line-edge irregularity in the trench is copied into the copolymer. Chemoepitaxy needs less area for the same final CD and tolerates more design freedom because it does not demand exact width matching, but it needs a dedicated chemical-patterning material stack and is far more sensitive to surface-energy variation across the wafer. imec has run both on PS-b-PMMA at a 14 nm half-pitch on a 300 mm line and found a workable process window for each.

sections.heading: Raise χ for resolution and the process breaks
sections.body_md:
If PS-b-PMMA bottoms out near an 11 nm half-pitch because its blocks are only mildly incompatible, the obvious move is a more incompatible pair. It works, on paper: reported half-pitches run down to 8.5 nm for PS-b-PTMC, 7 nm for PS-b-PMA, 7.4 nm for P3HS-b-PDMS, and 5 nm lamellae for PVBD-b-PDSS.

The obvious move also breaks the process. Two blocks that dislike each other strongly also have very different surface energies, so during a thermal anneal one of them wets the air interface and the other wets the substrate, and the lamellae lie down flat instead of standing up through the film. Flat lamellae pattern nothing. The fixes are all extra process: solvent vapour annealing near room temperature, a spin-coated or vapour-deposited top coat that neutralises the air interface, laser spike annealing in milliseconds, microwave annealing.

So high χ does not simply buy resolution. It trades a hotplate for a solvent-handling tool or a second deposited layer.
sections.deeper_md: High χ pays a second dividend that is easy to miss: etch contrast. The PS/PMMA pair is nearly useless here — an O₂ reactive-ion etch removes PMMA only about 2.5 times faster than polystyrene, which is barely enough to open the pattern. Pairs containing an inorganic block are dramatically better: polymers with an iron-containing block reach 1:20 to 1:50 after RIE power tuning, and PDMSB-b-PMMA about 15:1. The alternative for PS-b-PMMA is sequential infiltration synthesis — running ALD precursors into the PMMA domains to grow alumina inside them, converting a polymer with no etch selectivity into an oxide hard mask, removable afterwards in KOH.

sections.heading: The defects are thermodynamic, and etch will not remove them
sections.body_md:
A fab wants fewer than one killing defect per square centimetre. Directed self-assembly has never got there, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of cleanliness.

Some defects are residue: bridges between lines, collapsed lines, trapped bubbles. Those behave like ordinary process defects and respond to ordinary fixes. The hard ones are topological — dislocations, where a line terminates or merges where it should have run straight, and disclinations, where the local orientation rotates. These are not contamination. They are metastable states of the pattern, and the only way out of them is for chains to move far enough that the lines reconnect correctly, which takes anneal time the throughput budget does not have.

And pattern transfer cannot save you. An etch removes material; it has no way to decide that a line should have continued. A dislocation present after the anneal is present in the final metal.
sections.deeper_md: Because defect annihilation is a kinetic race, annealing schedule is a real lever. Jacobs and co-workers took 15 nm line-space PS-b-PMMA lamellae on chemically patterned substrates and annealed them with a scanned laser at 300–800 °C peak for dwell times of 1 to 10 ms — far above the material's decomposition temperature at steady state, survivable only because the dwell is short. Repeated laser passes cut defectivity by 60%; a single 10 ms laser pulse followed by a conventional hotplate anneal cut it by 80%. Their explanation is that near the order–disorder transition the chains are mobile enough to re-register against the template, which is the step a lower-temperature bake never completes.

sections.heading: What it is actually for now
sections.body_md:
The 2012 version of this story was pitch multiplication: use self-assembly to get resolution a 193 nm immersion scanner could not reach, and skip EUV. That version lost. Defectivity did not fall fast enough and EUV arrived.

The current version is narrower and more plausible. EUV's dominant error source is stochastic — randomness in photon arrival and in resist chemistry, which Chris Mack of Fractilia has put at more than half of a high-volume manufacturer's patterning error budget. Those errors show up as wiggle and width variation on lines that are otherwise correctly placed. A block copolymer has one thing it does extremely well: it enforces its own period. Coat it over a printed EUV line pattern and it rectifies it, pulling edges back toward the copolymer's equilibrium spacing rather than multiplying anything. Intel has demonstrated this as DSA-enhanced EUV multipatterning at an 18 nm final metal pitch.

The design constraint has not moved, though. Self-assembly makes periodic patterns — lines or holes on a grid — which suits DRAM and arrays, and leaves logic needing DSA-aware layout.
sections.deeper_md: Metrology is the quieter obstacle. Before etch, the two blocks offer almost no contrast to a CD-SEM or an optical tool, so the pattern is easiest to measure after transfer, which is precisely too late to rework. Scatterometry — fitting a diffraction spectrum to a model of the profile — is the usual answer, and imec has tried convolutional detection on SEM images of hexagonal contact-hole arrays, reporting above 0.9 mean average precision with YOLOv8. Template design is still an open problem too: Zhou and co-workers published a Bayesian co-optimisation in 2025 that searches template shape and AB/AB blend composition together for sub-7 nm contact holes, with a curvature constraint added so the resulting templates are manufacturable.

glossary.definition: How strongly two polymer blocks dislike each other, per monomer contact. It falls as temperature rises, so the same material can be ordered at one bake temperature and disordered at another.
χ multiplied by the degree of polymerisation N. Microphase separation needs χN above about 10.5, which is why a shorter chain has to be built from more incompatible blocks to order at all.
The full pitch the copolymer adopts with no guidance, scaling roughly as χ^(1/6)·N^(2/3). The usable printed feature is about half of it, so a 22 nm L₀ gives an 11 nm half-pitch.
Directing assembly with etched topography: a trench two to five times the final critical dimension, whose floor is chemically neutral and one of whose sidewalls preferentially wets one block.

Directing assembly on a flat surface carrying chemical stripes — typically cross-linked polystyrene beside a neutral brush — so one block anchors to the stripe and the rest of the pattern registers outward from it.
Getting several final features out of one printed guide feature, because the copolymer subdivides the guided region at its own period. The multiplication factor is how many periods fit in the guide.

Running atomic-layer-deposition precursors into one block of an already-assembled film to grow a metal oxide inside it, converting a polymer with almost no etch contrast into a hard mask with a great deal of it.

A line that terminates or merges where it should have run straight. Unlike a bridge or a residue defect it cannot be etched away, because the error is in the pattern itself rather than in leftover material.

foundations.try_this: Do the arithmetic that sets the floor, then go and measure the other half of it. From χ ≈ 0.039 for PS-b-PMMA at 150 °C and the χN > 10.5 ordering threshold in Chen and Xiong's review, the shortest chain that will still microphase-separate is about N = 270 monomers — which is the real reason this material bottoms out near an 11 nm half-pitch, and why the field went hunting for higher χ. Then read the pattern-transfer section of the same review, note the 1:2.5 O₂-RIE selectivity between polystyrene and PMMA, and measure what selectivity the club's own RIE gets between photoresist and thermal oxide. Those are the same kind of number, and one of them you can have by Friday.
